title: transfer POST /api/delegations: parentDelegationId comes straight from the body and nothing ties it to the caller
description:
**BLUF:** `POST /api/delegations` takes the delegator from the authenticated user but passes `req.body.parentDelegationId` straight through, and the service checks only that the parent allows sub-delegation, has depth left and holds the permissions asked for; nothing compares the caller with the parent's delegatee, so any signed-in caller who knows a parent delegation id can create a child delegation under it. High. Priority as ruled by Wednesday (ANSWER 2026-11-06T03:40:16Z). Evidence class: READ ONLY at origin develop; the route was not run.

**Where**, at origin develop `45d2edc73aa9` (read 2026-11-06 by Seat S 27th with git show and git grep in a shallow scratch clone of origin develop `45d2edc73aa9`; nothing was run):

* `Blockchain/Dev/services/transfer/src/routes/delegations.ts` lines 60 to 80: `delegatorId` is read from `req.user` (line 64, 401 if absent); `createDelegationSchema.parse(req.body)` runs at line 69; the call at lines 71 to 75 passes `delegatorId`, the parsed body and `req.body.parentDelegationId` (line 74) to `createDelegation`.
* `Blockchain/Dev/services/transfer/src/services/delegationService.ts`: `createDelegation(delegatorId, request, parentDelegationId?)` from about line 187. The parent branch (lines 200 to 215) loads the parent, requires `canSubDelegate`, requires `currentDepth < maxDelegationDepth`, and requires the requested types to be a subset of the parent's. No line compares `delegatorId` with the parent's delegatee.
* I found no document-owner check in the route (lines 60 to 80) or in `createDelegation` up to line 220; I did not read past line 220.

**For the owner to decide:** require the caller to be the parent delegation's delegatee, and require ownership of the document for a top-level delegation.

**NOT measured:** the route at runtime; a real database; a gateway path; the service after line 220.

**Source:** Seat W 29th's QUESTION mail to Wednesday of 2026-11-06T02:47:04Z (section 5, item iii), re-read by Seat S 27th at the lines above.

**Board search before filing (2026-11-06, Seat S 27th, board_search tool, both controls held: 'msgpackr' hit KS-1379 among open tickets, a random token hit 0):** `parentDelegationId` returned 0 candidates; `createDelegation` 0 candidates. KS-1703 names a delegation read in its GET-by-id list; it does not cover creation.

title: transfer POST /api/transfers: the initiator names both parties in the body and nothing checks the caller is the current owner
description:
**BLUF:** `POST /api/transfers` (and `/api/transfers/initiate`) takes `currentOwnerId` and `newOwnerId` from the request body, validates only that each is a GUID, and copies both into the new transfer, so an authenticated caller can open a transfer that names someone else as the owner and themselves as the recipient. High. Priority as ruled by Wednesday (ANSWER 2026-11-06T03:40:16Z). Evidence class: READ ONLY at origin develop; the handler was not run.

**Where**, at origin develop `45d2edc73aa9` (read 2026-11-06 by Seat S 27th with git show and git grep in a shallow scratch clone of origin develop `45d2edc73aa9`; nothing was run):

* `Blockchain/Dev/services/transfer/src/index.ts` lines 375 and 376: `currentOwnerId: z.string().guid()` and `newOwnerId: z.string().guid()`. Line 528: `const initiatedBy = ((req as any).user?.userId as string) || data.currentOwnerId;` so the authenticated user feeds only `initiatedBy`, and the body's owner is the fallback. Lines 542 and 543 copy `data.currentOwnerId` and `data.newOwnerId` into the transfer. Lines 602 and 603 mount the handler on both paths. Nothing in the handler compares `currentOwnerId` with the caller or checks who owns `documentId`.
* Lines 580 to 582 create notifications for both named parties, so the named owner receives an approval-required notice for a transfer they did not start.

**Why it matters for KS-2038:** KS-2038 (the transfer routes approve, reject, execute and cancel admit any signed-in caller and take the actor from the body) depends on this ticket: any rule it adopts about who may act on a transfer reads `currentOwnerId` from the stored transfer, and this route lets the initiator set that value freely. The rule itself is not decided here and nothing in this ticket states it; the decision card for it is still open.

**Seat W 29th's reading (relayed in Wednesday's brief; not re-run by Seat S 27th):** binding `currentOwnerId` to the caller turns an existing object-authorization cell red, because that cell creates a transfer with an owner id that is not the caller.

**For the owner to decide:** bind `currentOwnerId` to the authenticated caller (or check ownership of `documentId`) at initiate, and refuse otherwise.

**NOT measured:** the handler at runtime; a real database; a gateway path; whether another service already checks document ownership before the gateway forwards this call.

**Source:** Seat W 29th's QUESTION mail to Wednesday of 2026-11-06T02:47:04Z (section 5, item i), re-read by Seat S 27th at the lines above.

**Board search before filing (2026-11-06, Seat S 27th, board_search tool, both controls held: 'msgpackr' hit KS-1379 among open tickets, a random token hit 0):** `initiateTransferHandler` returned 0 candidates. `currentOwnerId` and `newOwnerId` each returned one open literal hit, KS-1703, which names the two fields as part of the row a GET-by-id route returns; its scope is GET-by-id routes, not the initiate handler. Closed hits KS-466, KS-474 and KS-475 are earlier, different defects.

**BLUF:** Gate 229, on PR 2048 (KS-2038), measured what KS-2049's trust root means for the new caller rule, and routes two findings here. Facts only: (F2) a false record can walk to `completed` and an inheritance form reaches `executing`, because the rule checks the caller against the party names the opener typed; (F3) nobody can now remove a false record. Nothing here changes this ticket's priority or scope.

* **F2, graded HIGH by the gate, for routing to this ticket (MEASURED AT RUNTIME at head cd44efa7ebb3 against the base, real authenticator, no gateway):**
  * Better than the base: naming a victim as owner and yourself as recipient no longer lets the caller execute (base 200, head 403). Strangers are out of other people's transfers.
  * Same as the base: one caller who names themselves as owner and recipient walks a simple transfer alone, and it goes on to `completed` after the 2 s timer, with a `mock_tx_` hash and the notification text "You are now the owner". Two accounts also walk it. The gate notes that Seat W 29th's note said "to executing"; measured, it goes further.
  * Same as the base, and not in that note: an inheritance that names a real owner as deceased, the attacker as executor and an accomplice as beneficiary reaches `executing` with no act by the owner, whose reject then reads 400. One caller holding both inheritance roles stops at 1 of 2. This form does not survive a restart, because the executor is not stored.
  * In the gate's words, the rule means a lot for records opened honestly and nothing for a false one: "owner" is whoever the opener typed, and `documentId` is checked against no holder. The gate asks that this ticket's scope name the inheritance form.
  * Reach, READ ONLY by the gate: the transfer service makes no outbound HTTP call and no other service reads `svc_transfers`, so a false record plus its notifications stands as the reach.
* **F3, graded LOW-MEDIUM, MEASURED AT RUNTIME:** nobody can now remove a false record. The true holder of a document that the record does not name reads 404 on reject (base 200). A platform administrator reads 404 on reject and cancel (the base answered 400 only because the holder had just rejected; any caller could act at the base). The "no admin override" clause is Kam's; the gate records that this cost is not stated on his card.
* **Source:** gate 229 verdict, findings F2 and F3: `/Volumes/DevMASTER/WEDNESDAY/0_Brain/reference/2026-11-06_gate229-tier1-pr2048-ks2038/verdict.md` (a coordinator-local file). title: Pre-push cost: leg 14's 116 shell suites run one after another and are 90 to 92 percent of every push, and no other leg is timed
description:
BLUF: Every push that changes Blockchain/Dev runs all 16 preflight legs inside the push lock. Leg 14, the 116 shell suites, is 90 to 92 percent of it (948 of 1033 s, 990 of 1096 s, 1102 of 1213 s on three pushes read on 2026-11-06), they run strictly one after another, and no other leg is timed, so the other 85 to 111 s of each push is unattributed. At 03:26Z the push queue held 19 live tickets; at about 19 minutes a push that is several hours before the last of them reaches a gate.

One test pass, three items:

1. Per-leg timing. Blockchain/Dev/scripts/preflight/preflight.sh prints one line per leg for all 16 legs at the verdict, in leg order, each marked ran or skipped, with its seconds and a line stating the ratio of legs timed (16/16). The existing PREFLIGHT PASSED and PREFLIGHT FAILED lines, the legs ran count, the exit codes, the skip accounting and the shell suites wall-clock line stay byte-for-byte what they are. A failed run still prints the table.
2. Parallel suites, conditional on a measurement. First measure on this host whether the 116 suites collide when run side by side (fixed ports, shared postgres sockets, fixed names under /tmp) and what the saving is at several worker caps. Only if a safe set exists, Blockchain/Dev/scripts/run-shell-suites.sh runs it in parallel under a worker cap with buffered output printed in suite order. Every suite still runs. The pass, fail and skip rule, the empty-run refusal, the git environment clearing, the short TMPDIR substitution and --list and --check-unreached stay as they are; a worker cap of 1 reproduces today's serial output. New assertion: passed plus failed plus skipped must equal the suites reached. INT and TERM stop every running worker. bash 3.2 only. If the saving is small beside the added risk, item 2 is not raised and the numbers go on this ticket.
3. The push rehearsal runs leg 1 under the driver's own TMPDIR, so a hook-only failure like Seat V 24th's (a 121-byte tsx socket path against macOS's 104, lock held 18.6 minutes) shows in a rehearsal. This is a corrected tool copy in the seat's record folder, not part of the PR.

Not in scope: running the preflight outside the lock or pushing with --no-verify (Kam's card secuura-push-queue-prerun-preflight-1106, option a, is open; this work is its default, option b). This work reaches only branches cut after it merges, because the hook and the runner run from each pushing worktree's own tracked copy.

Source: Wednesday's push-queue cost report, 0_Brain/reference/2026-11-06_push-queue-cost/report.md (section 1 table and the UNMEASURED list).

Board search before filing (title and description, archived included, Secuura-PK): shell suites wall-clock 0 hits; per-leg timing 0; step() timing 0; worker cap 0; TMPDIR with rehears 0. Positive controls: run-shell-suites 28 hits, push queue 2 hits. Negative control, a nonsense symbol, 0 hits.

title: anchoring answers 202 during a database outage and the anchor has no row after recovery
description:
**BLUF:** In a Postgres outage on a disposable stack, anchoring answered 202 to 9 of 25 `POST /api/anchors` requests, and after recovery `anchor_store` held no row created after the stop. A 202 tells the caller its anchor was accepted. Split out of KS-2045 on Wednesday's ruling, because a crash loop and a 202 with no stored row are separate fixes. Nothing here is fixed.

## Measured

Seat U 16th, 2026-11-06, on throw-away stack `u16` built from develop `2fd6d529573c`, `NODE_ENV=development`, mock anchoring with no wallet. Not on a box. Postgres stopped 03:07:23Z for about 100 s, pgbouncer left running. A prober on the stack's internal network sent one `POST /api/anchors` every 4 s directly to anchoring, with a connector JWT minted on that stack.

* **9 of 25 answered 202.** The other 16 got connection, DNS or socket errors while the process was restarting (KS-2045).
* `anchor_store` **read at 03:11:30Z, about 2 minutes after Postgres was healthy: 0 rows created after the stop.** The newest row is 03:07:22.643Z. The 2 rows created just before the stop are there as the control, and the table holds 15 in all.
* **Anchoring's log in the outage:** `Database unavailable — using in-memory fallback` 9 times, `Anchor created` 9 times (2 more before the stop). The counts match the 9 responses; the prober kept statuses and not ids, so they were not matched one to one.
* **Each of those 9** `Anchor created` **lines is followed by the process crash in KS-2045 within 1 to 4 ms** (03:07:27.904Z to 03:08:42.469Z), so in this run no process that wrote one lived on. The row read is after the last restart.

## Read at source, not run

`Blockchain/Dev/services/anchoring/src/index.ts` at `2fd6d529573c`, in `dbPersistAnchor`:

* lines 1551 to 1552, a comment: "a failed persist must propagate so the handler returns a 5xx rather than a false 202".
* line 1553: `if (!isDbAvailable()) return { id: anchor.id, payloadTimestamp: payloadTimestampOf(anchor.metadataPayload) };`, which returns with no write.
* line 538: the handler calls it and carries on.

## UNMEASURED

* Whether anything later replays those anchors. The read came about 3 minutes after the last 202, and the stack was torn down at 03:13Z. That is why this ticket says "no row after recovery" and not "lost".
* How long an in-memory copy lives in a process that does not crash. Here each process crashed within 4 ms, so KS-2045 may be hiding what this path does on its own.
* Whether anything reaches a chain. This stack has no wallet, so nothing could from here; on a box, not measured.
* Kintsugi and demo, and `NODE_ENV=production`.
* The 202 bodies, and what a caller does on one. The prober kept statuses only.

## Searched before filing, 2026-11-06

Board search over titles, descriptions and comments, archived included:

* `using in-memory fallback`: open KS-1969 (auth sessions on Redis) and KS-2045 (where this was first written); closed KS-377.
* `dbPersistAnchor`: open KS-1384, KS-1385, KS-1644, KS-1652, KS-1664, KS-1916, KS-1919; closed KS-281, KS-489, KS-1633.
* `in-memory fallback`: open KS-772, KS-946, KS-1087, KS-1194, KS-1233, KS-1969, KS-2011 and KS-2045, plus 8 closed. By title these are about other subjects; I did not read them whole.

I read KS-1384, KS-1385, KS-1644, KS-1652, KS-1664, KS-1916, KS-1919, KS-281 and KS-377 for a write path with the database unavailable, and none owns this. KS-377 (Done) is nearest: the same fallback line, and its repro stops Postgres, but its subject is the latch at boot and its fix was retrying, not this 202.

Controls on the same instrument: `mobile/secuura-app` hit KS-1981 and a random token hit 0.

Evidence: `5_Project_History/2026-11-06_seatU-16th/evidence/crash_remeasure/` (`run.out`, `anchoring_log.txt`, `anchor_window.out`).

title: Postgres outage behind pgbouncer kills auth, anchoring, api-gateway and tenant-provisioning on an unhandled pg client error
description:
**BLUF:** On a disposable stack, stopping Postgres with pgbouncer still up crash-looped auth and anchoring and restarted api-gateway and tenant-provisioning once each, on an unhandled pg client error. Callers saw 504 then 502, not the designed 503. With pgbouncer stopped too, auth stayed up and answered 503. Anchoring answered 202 nine times during the outage and those anchors have no row after recovery. Nothing here is fixed.

Found by Seat U 16th, 2026-11-06, running KS-1477's owed check, on throw-away stack `u16` built from develop `2fd6d529573c`, `NODE_ENV=development`, compose's own pgbouncer and Postgres, mock anchoring. Not on a box.

## Measured: run 1, requests through nginx and the gateway to auth

Postgres stopped 02:53:43Z, started 02:56:09Z, pgbouncer left running.

* auth: 9 restarts in about 2 minutes, crashing 1 to 2 s after each boot until Postgres came back; 18 `Unhandled 'error' event` lines in its log.
* api-gateway: `Uncaught exception` with `Connection terminated unexpectedly`, then shutdown and restart, once, at 02:55:28Z.
* What callers saw for `POST /api/users/me/verification`: 504 `GATEWAY_TIMEOUT` after 60 s, then 502 `BAD_GATEWAY`. Never the 503.

## Measured: run 2, requests in flight directly to four services

Postgres stopped 03:07:23Z for about 100 s, pgbouncer left running. A short-lived prober on the stack's internal network sent one request to each service every 4 s, bypassing the gateway. The baseline with the database up answered 201, 202, 200 and 200.

| service | restarts | in its log | what the prober saw (25 requests) |
| -- | -- | -- | -- |
| anchoring | **10** | `Unhandled 'error' event` 10, `Connection terminated unexpectedly` 10 | 202 on 9; connection, DNS or socket errors on 16 |
| tenant-provisioning | **1** | `Unhandled 'error' event` 1, `terminating connection due to administrator command` | 500 on 23; connection refused on 2 |
| originate | 0 | none of these | 500 on 25, `Code: 08P01`, `server login has been failing` |
| security | 0 | none of these | 503 on 25 |

* auth and api-gateway had nothing in flight to them in run 2 and did not restart.
* **Anchoring's 202s:** read at 03:10Z, after recovery, `anchor_store` holds 0 rows created after the stop; its newest row is 03:07:22Z, from the baseline, and the 2 baseline rows are there as the control. Its log says `Database unavailable — using in-memory fallback` 9 times. So 9 anchors were accepted with 202 and have no row. Whether that is this defect or its own is not decided here.
* Every service read healthy again within about a minute of Postgres returning.

## Discriminating control

With pgbouncer **and** Postgres stopped, so no established connection can be cut: auth logged 0 crashes and stayed up, including when restarted during the outage (the in-memory fallback line once), and answered 503 `SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE` every time. Only auth was driven in this arm.

## The stack, verbatim, from auth

```
throw er; // Unhandled 'error' event
Error: Connection terminated unexpectedly
    at Connection.<anonymous> (/app/node_modules/pg/lib/client.js:204:73)
Emitted 'error' event on Client instance at:
    at Client._handleErrorEvent (/app/node_modules/pg/lib/client.js:422:10)
```

It holds no application frames.

## A reading, not measured

* It reads as a pg client checked out of a pool when pgbouncer cuts its connection ("server login has been failing"). The pool-level `on('error')` handlers would not cover a checked-out client.
* auth and the gateway died with a request in flight to them in run 1 and did not in run 2. That suggests in-flight work is the trigger; two runs do not establish it.

## UNMEASURED

* The call site in each service.
* Kintsugi and demo. Compose has the same pgbouncer; nothing was tried on a box.
* `NODE_ENV=production`.
* Every service not on this stack. Run 2 clears nothing: originate and security did not die under one request every 4 s, and a heavier or longer load was not tried.

## Searched before filing, 2026-11-06

Board search over titles, descriptions and comments, archived included:

* `Connection terminated unexpectedly`: open KS-1587 and KS-1960, closed KS-1188, none about this.
* `Unhandled 'error' event`: closed KS-1185 only.
* `pool.on('error')`, `client.on('error')`, `server login has been failing`, `terminating connection due to administrator command`: 0 hits each.
* `crash-loop`: open KS-485, KS-1079, KS-1982, none about a database outage.

Controls on the same instrument: `mobile/secuura-app` hit KS-1981 and a random token hit 0.

Evidence: `5_Project_History/2026-11-06_seatU-16th/evidence/ks1477/` and `evidence/crash_remeasure/`.

nodes.body:
**BLUF:** Facts only. Anchoring's 202s with no stored row now have their own ticket, KS-2046, which owns them; this ticket keeps the crash. Wednesday ruled the split on 2026-11-06, because they are separate fixes.

* **A correction to this ticket's description:** the `anchor_store` read it gives as 03:10Z was at 03:11:30Z, from the output file's timestamp. Nothing else in that read changes.
* **Measured and not split out, by the same ruling:** in run 2, originate answers 500 (`Code: 08P01`) where security answers 503, on the same outage.
* **Also measured, from the saved logs:** in run 2 each of anchoring's 9 `Anchor created` lines is followed by this crash within 1 to 4 ms, and one further crash came at the stop itself with none before it. That is 10 crashes in all.

title: transfer service: reject and approve admit any signed-in caller of any tenant and take the actor from the body
description:
## BLUF

`POST /api/transfers/:id/reject` and `POST /api/transfers/:id/approve` in the transfer service have **no caller check**. Any signed-in caller of any tenant, with any role, can reject or approve any transfer, and the actor that gets recorded is whatever the request body says (`rejectorId` and `rejectorRole` on reject, `approverId` and `approverRole` on approve). Found by QA gate 215 (finding F1, High) while gating five merged PRs. It predates PR 1408 and is not caused by it. Facts only; no fix shape is proposed here, and a design seat follows.

Gate verdict: `/Volumes/DevMASTER/WEDNESDAY/0_Brain/reference/2026-11-06_gate215-old-credential-prs/verdict.md`.

## Where (re-read by me at origin develop `b57fe1853c22`; the gate's line numbers were from `7ad5a8b4bdf7` and still hold)

* `Blockchain/Dev/services/transfer/src/index.ts:449` `app.use('/api', jwtAuthenticate());` is the only guard in the service.
* Reject: the route starts at `:748`; the body is parsed at `:750`; `:763` `rejectorId: data.rejectorId,` and `:764` `rejectorRole: data.rejectorRole,` record the actor from the body.
* Approve: the route starts at `:673`; `:693` and `:694` record `approverId` and `approverRole` from the body; the duplicate check at `:687` compares only the body's `approverId`.
* Between the start of the reject route and the state change there is **0 match for** `req.user`**,** `tenant` **or** `role` (case-sensitive; read by me over lines 748 to 801). The only case-insensitive hit is the body field `rejectorRole` itself. The gate read the same at the tip and at `2c27ddfee^`, which is why it is older than PR 1408.
* The gateway adds authentication only: `Blockchain/Dev/services/api-gateway/src/routes/proxy.ts:1108-1111` mounts `/api/transfers` behind `authenticateToken(true)` and the proxy, with no tenant or role check (read).

## Measured by gate 215 (not by me), at handler level with a mocked authenticator

title: Security: a demoted, deleted or gone user whose token still says ADMIN can still mint and revoke tenant-level API keys (same on base)
description:
## BLUF

A user who is no longer a live ADMIN of tenant T (demoted, deleted, deactivated, suspended, pending, invited, inactive, users row gone, or users row in another tenant) but whose still-valid token says ADMIN of T can **mint an API key with no organisation (a tenant-level key: 201, key created)** and **revoke a tenant-level key (200, key revoked)**. Identical on base. Found by QA gate 214 on PRs 2029, 2030 and 2031 (finding F2). It is outside Kam's ruling, which is about scope rows (card `secuura-ks1585-scope-rows-on-admin-change-1105`, option b). Facts only; nothing is built.

Gate verdict: `/Volumes/DevMASTER/WEDNESDAY/0_Brain/reference/2026-11-06_gate214-ks1585-ks1377-pr2029-2031/verdict.md`.

## Where (read at PR 2030's head `f107b9688445`; line numbers shift once it merges)

* `Blockchain/Dev/packages/shared/src/security/keyRevokePolicy.ts:263-267`: for a scoped admin role, an unqualified target (no organisation) returns `{ allow: true, reason: 'same-tenant' }` before any scope or liveness check. The comment above it (about `:257`) says so on purpose: an unqualified target "falls through to the tenant verdict".
* `Blockchain/Dev/services/security/src/index.ts:1368` (the mint decision) and `:1645` (the revoke decision), both fed the caller from the token.
* The organisation-naming refusal at `index.ts:1392` ends "omit organizationId to mint a tenant-level key": the 403 itself names the way around it.

## Measured by gate 214 (not by me), real routes on PostgreSQL 15.19

* Token says ADMIN of T, one scope row {A1} in T. For every non-live user above: **mint with no organisation 201 and a key created; revoke of a tenant-level key 200 and the key revoked.** Same on base and on PR 2030. Evidence in the gate folder: `runs/evidence/table_p2030.json`, `table_base.json`.
* The same users naming an organisation: base mint 201 and revoke 200; PR 2030 mint 403 and revoke 403. So PR 2030 closes the organisation path only.
* A live admin and another tenant's live admin: unchanged.

## Why it matters (read, not measured)

PR 2030's own code comment names the harm: a token issued before the change (they live up to a day) still minted and revoked. That harm survives for organisation-less keys, and PR 2030's NOT-done list does not name it.

## Not measured

* **Whether a tenant-level key reaches more than an organisation key**: what a key with no organisation can do that a key naming one cannot.
* The deployed boxes (no box read): the real token lifetime, and whether any user is in a non-live state with a live token today.
* Whether the gateway checks user liveness before it forwards to the security service (not read).

## Open question (a decision, not made here)

Should a tenant-level mint and revoke require the same live-ADMIN test the organisation arm now applies? After PR 2030 merges that test exists as one exported fragment, `LIVE_ADMIN_USER_PREDICATE` in `services/security/src/adminScope.ts`. Not built; Wednesday decides whether it goes to Kam.

Filed by Seat G 28th from gate 214's F2, on Wednesday's instruction (ANSWER 2026-11-06 01:15:23Z). Related: KS-1585 (the ticket of PR 2030), KS-1570 (the ADMIN-role ruling).

title: api-gateway: after a Redis eviction GET /api/admin/settings and GET /api/verification/policy read only Redis and serve the defaults, so a settings round trip can replace the stored allow-lists
description:
**BLUF:** In api-gateway at develop `07a2d62be6a0`, `GET /api/admin/settings` reads the `platform-settings` key from Redis directly, not through the settings store. After an eviction it serves the four default categories with no `integrations` key, although the stored record still holds the configured settings. `PUT /api/admin/settings` does read the stored record on a miss and merges `{ ...defaults, ...existing, ...body }`, so a body key replaces the stored key whole. A client that saves what the GET showed, with `integrations: []`, replaces the stored allow-lists with an empty list. `GET /api/verification/policy` makes the same direct Redis read. This is Seat E 35th's candidate 1 for PR 2001 (its "item 7").

Source: /Volumes/DevMASTER/WEDNESDAY/0_Brain/reference/2026-11-04_gate189-ks1256-pr2001/ready_2001.txt, CANDIDATES FOR FILING, item 1.

## Where (read at develop `07a2d62be6a0`, `Blockchain/Dev/services/api-gateway/src/routes/admin.ts`)

* Lines 1150 to 1159: `redisService.getNotificationSettings('platform-settings') || {}`, laid over `PLATFORM_SETTINGS_DEFAULTS`.
* Lines 1184 to 1197: the PUT reads through `readPlatformSettings` (stored record on a miss) and merges with `...body` last.
* Lines 1216 to 1228: `GET /api/verification/policy` reads Redis directly and answers the built-in defaults on a miss or a throw.
* The defaults object (`Blockchain/Dev/services/api-gateway/src/services/settingsStore.ts` lines 38 to 43) holds `general`, `security`, `notifications` and `blockchain`; no `integrations`.

## Measured

Not by gate 189: its findings G189-F1 to F7 do not include this. The READY mail lists it as a candidate. This seat read the code only.

KS-1256 already names the two direct readers: its comment `de80f9b8` (2026-10-06) lists them as "the other readers", and its comment `6d4b1366` (2026-11-04, Seat W 24th, read at `ee1e1b832115`, "read, not measured") restates them by function: `GET /api/admin/settings` "a missing key serves the defaults as if they were stored", and `GET /api/verification/policy` "a missing key, or a throw, answers the defaults", with the line "Left open: ... The other readers are listed above." That text predates PR 2001. What this ticket records is the state at `07a2d62be6a0`: both direct readers are unchanged, and PR 2001 changed `PUT /api/admin/settings` to read the stored record on a miss, which is what makes a round trip of the GET's content replace the stored allow-lists.

## Grade

Low, this seat's judgement. It needs an admin client that round-trips the whole document, and whether one exists is not measured.

## Not measured

* Any run of the GET after an eviction, or of the round trip.
* Whether any admin UI or script sends the whole document back, or sends `integrations`.
* Whether a configured `verification` category is stored in any environment.
* This seat ran no test and no service; the code facts are reads of a depth-1 clone at `07a2d62be6a0`.

## Related

* KS-1256 (PR 2001's ticket); PR 2001 merged as `6a36d41b9852`.
* Board search before filing (team Secuura-PK, archived included): `api/admin/settings` 8 open (KS-485, KS-772, KS-1204, KS-1230, KS-1231, KS-1233, KS-1256, KS-1262), 0 closed; `api/verification/policy` 2 open (KS-736, KS-1256), 0 closed; `readPlatformSettings` 0 and 0; `PLATFORM_SETTINGS_DEFAULTS` 0 and 0. Control: `svc_gateway_settings` and `api/admin/settings` hit in the same run (2 and 8 open). KS-1256 names the two direct readers (above); KS-736 (mount-auth scoring) appears in the policy hits and this seat read its title only. This ticket is filed as its own ticket so that KS-1256 can close; the round trip with the changed PUT is not named in KS-1256.

title: Every read of svc_nft_certificates.public_fields runs JSON.parse on an already-parsed JSONB array, so a stored NFT certificate cannot be read back
description:
BLUF: In the nft-certificate service, every read of the `public_fields` column runs `JSON.parse` on a value the Postgres driver has already parsed. The column is JSONB, so the driver returns an array, `JSON.parse` of an array throws, and a stored certificate cannot be read back. The write path stores a JSON array, so this reaches every row the service writes itself. The rows are intact in the database; they are unreadable through the service. Priority High (the brief's suggestion, and my grade): the failure sits on the read path of every stored certificate, and nothing short of a code change works around it.

Source: /Volumes/DevMASTER/!CODING/Secuura/Blockchain/5_Project_History/2026-11-04_seatW-27th/HANDOVER.md (lines 28 to 31) and /Volumes/DevMASTER/!CODING/Secuura/Blockchain/5_Project_History/2026-11-04_seatW-27th/evidence/search_nft_jsonb.out. Seat W 27th found it on a disposable stack (w27) at ee1e1b832115. I read the code at origin/develop 035685291b9d myself.

What I read (code, not a run):

* `Blockchain/Dev/migrations/002_verification-tiers.sql` line 796, inside `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS svc_nft_certificates` (line 784): `public_fields JSONB DEFAULT '[]'`. No other file under `Blockchain/Dev/migrations` names the column (searched `public_fields`).
* `Blockchain/Dev/services/nft-certificate/src/services/minting.service.ts` line 76 writes `JSON.stringify(cert.publicFields || [])` into that column.
* The same file reads it with `JSON.parse(row.public_fields || '[]')` at line 123 (`loadFromDb`, the startup load, which selects every row of `svc_nft_certificates`) and at lines 505, 592 and 678. The row type declares `public_fields: string`, which is not what a JSONB column returns.
* `loadFromDb` runs the parse inside its loop. The first row that holds an array makes it throw into the function's catch, so no later row is loaded.

What Seat W 27th measured on w27 (disposable stack, ee1e1b832115): the log lines `DB get user certificates failed` and `DB get wallet certificates failed`, each with `Unexpected end of JSON input`. A row whose `public_fields` is NULL reads fine.

Fix shape (not chosen here): accept the value the driver returns for JSONB (an array) at the four read sites, or make the column text and keep the stringify. Either needs a test that round-trips a stored row.

Not measured: a run of this code by me; how many rows `svc_nft_certificates` holds on kintsugi or the demo environment; whether any deployed environment overrides the driver's JSONB parser; what the three DB read paths return to the caller after the catch (W 27th's log lines are the only evidence of the failure itself).
Board search (this seat, 2026-11-05): `public_fields` 0 open and 0 closed literal hits; `minting.service` with `JSON.parse` 0; `Unexpected end of JSON input` 0. Seat W 27th named KS-1843 as the nearest neighbour, a different defect.

title: auth: the breached-password check (isPasswordBreached, pen-test F-12 item 3) has no caller, so sign-up, reset and change-password accept a breached password
description:
**BLUF:** in the auth service, `isPasswordBreached` (`Blockchain/Dev/services/auth/src/services/password.ts:130`, the HaveIBeenPwned k-anonymity check) has **no caller anywhere in the repository**. The file's own header (lines 5-15) titles its list after pen-test F-12 and makes this check item 3. So sign-up, password reset and change-password accept a password that appears in a public breach list, provided it passes `checkPasswordStrength`, and the `HIBP_ENABLED` switch controls nothing. Pre-existing. Measured by QA gate 161 (finding G161-F2, rated HIGH); the pen-test report itself is UNREAD, so whether F-12 item 3 was accepted as residual is not known.

**Authority.** Kam, live board 2026-11-03 15:53:02, card `secuura-hibp-breach-check-never-runs-1103`, verbatim: "Decision secuura-hibp-breach-check-never-runs-1103: a — Wire it in: refuse a breached password at sign-up, reset and change-password; if the breach service is down, allow it (as written)". Option a's detail, verbatim: "A Secuura seat files the High ticket and builds it behind the existing HIBP_ENABLED switch, tier 1 Opus gate. The user sees 'this password has appeared in a data breach, choose another'. Outage = allowed, so sign-ups never depend on a third party."

**The code** (read at develop `10edf375ac31` with `git show`, by Seat F 27th):

* `password.ts:130-162`: sends `https://api.pwnedpasswords.com/range/<first 5 hex of the SHA-1>` with `Add-Padding` and a 2 s timeout, matches the suffix locally, and answers false on a non-200 or a throw (fails open). `HIBP_ENABLED` is read only at `:131`, and only the string `false` disables it, so the default is ON.
* Call sites: 0 (`git grep isPasswordBreached` hits only its definition, one KS-1868 test and two KS-1868 docs fragments). Positive control: `verifyPassword` has 4 call sites (gate 161).
* `HIBP_ENABLED` is set in 0 of 46 env-example and compose files (names only; positive control `REDIS_URL` hits 12). Once wired in, the check is ON in local, demo and every team build.
* Validation order today: register `routes/auth.ts:161` (strength 422 at `:204`, hash at `:209`); reset `routes/auth.ts:848` (strength 422 at `:852`, token at `:857-867`, hash at `:877`, token consumed at `:931`); change-password `routes/users.ts:975` (current password 400 at `:989`, strength 422 at `:991`, hash at `:996`).
* The catch at `password.ts:151-159` logs the thrown value's message text (the logging class of `KS-1868`).

**Remedy (option a), ruled split by Wednesday 2026-11-03:** call `isPasswordBreached` at all three routes, after the existing strength check, behind `HIBP_ENABLED`; a breached password gets 422 with Kam's sentence; an unreachable breach service allows the password. Only the 5-character hash prefix leaves the process. No test calls the real service. Two PRs, both "Refs" this ticket: **B1** = register + reset (reset checks after the token and user are validated, so a refusal never consumes the token); **B2** = change-password (`routes/users.ts`), queued behind open PRs #1798 (`KS-1459`) and #1796 (`KS-1458`), which touch the same file. TIER 1, Opus gate. Nothing merges or deploys from this ticket alone.

**Before this deploys (consequences, as ruled):** demo and every local stack will call the real HaveIBeenPwned range API at sign-up and reset, because no env file sets `HIBP_ENABLED`; an e2e flow or seed that registers with a breached test password will get 422.

**Not in scope (candidates only):** `POST /api/users/admin/create` (`routes/users.ts:584`, hash at `:645`) also sets a password and runs no strength check either; it is not one of Kam's three routes. Whether failing open on an outage stays the policy is ruled (it does).

**Duplicate search** (Linear searchIssues, 2026-11-03 \~05:2xZ, team Secuura-PK): `isPasswordBreached` and `HIBP` hit only `KS-1868` (the logging class); `HaveIBeenPwned` 0; `pwnedpasswords` only `KS-951` (the default-password CI gate). Neither is a wire-in ticket. Positive control: `accountLockout` finds `KS-1967`. Related, not duplicates: `KS-1796` (change-password publishes no 422 in the spec), `KS-1854` (reset has no rate limit of its own).

Source: `/Volumes/DevMASTER/WEDNESDAY/0_Brain/reference/2026-11-03_gate161-ks1868-pr1978/verdict.md`, finding G161-F2.

Register checks after the strength rules; reset after the token and the account are proven and before anything is hashed, written or consumed, so a refused reset leaves the link usable.
* If the breach service throws, times out (2 s) or answers non-200, the password is allowed, as ruled. Only the first 5 characters of the SHA-1 are sent. `HIBP_ENABLED=false` still turns the check off; the auth test setup now sets it to false when unset, so no test reaches the real service.
* Evidence: red first, 10 of 28 cells fail by assertion on develop and 28 of 28 pass with the change; 17 of 17 mutants killed; whole auth suite 1,622 of 1,623 on develop (the 1 is the known flake) and 1,641 of 1,641 with the change, both under a guard that counted 0 requests to the breach service. Host Node v26.8.1, not an LTS line.
* Not done here: change-password (B2, waiting on open PRs 1798 and 1796, which edit `routes/users.ts`); `POST /api/users/admin/create`, which sets a password with neither check (candidate); the OpenAPI 422 descriptions of the two routes (candidate). Nothing deployed.

title: referral: duplicate milestone reward rows the re-award bug already stored stay stored and still count as pending rewards
description:
**BLUF:** The referral re-award bug (KS 1956) stored duplicate CLAIMABLE milestone reward rows in `svc_referral_milestones_rewards`: the same user and milestone, more than once. The repair in pull request 1979 stops NEW duplicates; it removes none. The rows already stored stay stored, and `GET /api/rewards/user` still counts every one of them as a pending reward that can be claimed. Any cleanup is a DATA change and Kam's decision later; this ticket proposes nothing destructive. Pre-existing, High (QA gate 162).

## What is measured

* **QA gate 162** (2026-11-03, real PostgreSQL 15, the real referral service over HTTP, on pull request 1979): before the repair the same user and milestone reached 2 to 4 rows across its cells. After the repair, new checks add none, and the progress row records each milestone once. Every duplicate row stored earlier is still there and is still a pending reward.
* **QA gate 153** (2026-11-03): `GET /api/rewards/user` shows these rows as pending with `canClaim: true`, which inflates the balance a user sees.

## What is not measured

* Whether production has `svc_referral_milestones_rewards` at all (the repo has no DDL for it, KS 1956), and if so how many duplicate rows it holds. Nothing in the repo shows production's schema or data.
* Claiming: `POST /api/rewards/claim` reads `svc_referral_rewards` only, so milestone rewards cannot be claimed through it (read, not run). No money moves inside the referral service.

## A first step that changes nothing

Size it, read-only: count rows per (`user_id`, `source_id`) where `source_type = 'MILESTONE'` and the count is above 1, on whichever database holds the table. What to do with any duplicates found is for Kam to decide; it is not proposed here.

## Related

KS 1956 (the re-award bug and its repair, pull request 1979), KS 1957 (the owner and role check on the award routes, pull request 1980).

title: originate document signing: a sign, sign-cert or sign-wallet request can answer 500 after the signature or signed document is saved, and a retry duplicates it
description:
**BLUF:** In originate, `POST /api/documents/:id/sign`, `/:id/sign-cert` and `/:id/sign-wallet` can answer 500 after the signature, or the signed derived document, is already saved. A retry then saves a second one. This is pre-existing: it happens the same way for an ordinary Error at base, and pull request 1964 does not cause it. Found by QA gate 149 on PR 1964 (findings G149-F1 and G149-F2).

**What happens** (measured by gate 149: the six real document routes in their own Node process, with an in-memory documents model that rejects AFTER it has applied the write; the identical request is then retried with no fault):

* `POST /:id/sign` (`updateDocument` is the write): the signature is persisted and the status is `signed`, the caller gets 500, and the signing nonce is NOT consumed. A retry with the same body inside the 5-minute nonce window answers 200 and appends a SECOND signature entry (1 signature, then 2).
* `POST /:id/sign-cert` and `POST /:id/sign-wallet` (`saveDocument` is the write): a derived document with status `signed` is persisted, carrying the sigJson or sigWallet envelope. The caller gets 500 and no `document.versioned` event is published. A retry mints a second derived signed document (derived 1, then 2, one event). For sign-cert the orphaned envelope can be fetched from the public `GET /:id/sig-json` route.
* `POST /:id/sign/request`: not affected. Its only write is synchronous and nothing is awaited after it; an orphan nonce expires after 5 minutes.

**Same at base:** with an ordinary `Error('Connection terminated unexpectedly')` at base, and with each of six unreadable thrown values at the head of PR 1964, the persisted state and the retry result were identical in all 288 compared cells. At base an unreadable value was worse: the caller got no answer, and so was just as likely to retry.

**Suggested shapes (from the gate, not chosen here):**

* sign: consume the nonce before the write (delete it, write, restore it on a definite pre-commit failure), or make the append idempotent on (signerId, nonce).
* sign-cert and sign-wallet: an idempotency key, or a deterministic derived id with `conflictMode: 'skip'` keyed on (parent, signature).

**Not tested:** a real PostgreSQL or Prisma client (the documents and lifecycle tables were an in-memory model); a real ambiguous commit (modelled as "write applied, then reject"); the real `authenticate()` and the gateway hop; a real Redis event bus; Node 24 (host Node v26.8.1).

Related: `KS-1831` (the sign route: authorization, revoked status and no signature verified), `KS-1693` (the same sign-cert and sign-wallet routes: no provenance recorded for the derived document).

title: vc-issuer: revoke() swallows a failed DB UPDATE — the route answers 200, the row stays unrevoked, and a restart reloads it as valid
description:
**BLUF:** In vc-issuer, `credentialRepo.revoke()` swallows a failed database UPDATE and keeps the revoke only in memory: the route `POST /api/credentials/:id/revoke` answers 200 "revoked successfully", the database row stays UNrevoked, and after a restart `loadFromDb` loads it unrevoked, so the credential verifies as valid. Measured by gate 152 for an ordinary Error (its scenario C); the restart is read, not run. Pre-existing, not introduced by pull request 1968 ([https://github.com/Secuura/Distributed_Secuura/pull/1968](<https://github.com/Secuura/Distributed_Secuura/pull/1968>)); found by gate 152. Same fail-open family as KS-1958.

## What happens

* `Blockchain/Dev/services/vc-issuer/src/repositories/credentialRepo.ts`: when `revoke()`'s database UPDATE fails, the error is swallowed ("kept in memory"). The credential is revoked in this process's memory only.
* The route answers 200 "revoked successfully" although the database row is unchanged.
* After a restart, `loadFromDb` (the only place memory is filled from the database) loads the row unrevoked, and the credential verifies as valid (read, not run past the restart).

## Measured (gate 152, scenario C)

The real route and repository were run; only `../db` (an in-memory fake table that can fail its UPDATE) and the logger were replaced. With an ordinary Error on the UPDATE: the route answers 200 "revoked successfully", memory is revoked, the database row is not. Base and head (pull request 1968) behave the same.

## A hostile value at the same place (finding G152-F4, read from source and measured for revoke)

For a revoked Proxy or an Error with a throwing `message` getter on that UPDATE, the revoke answers 500 after memory is already revoked, because `revoke()`'s own catch (around line 502) still reads `err?.message` unguarded. Three sibling catches in the same file still do too: `store` (around line 98), `getReadableByHash` (around 324, the by-hash route's path) and `selectList` (around 413, the list route); `db.ts` `probeDb` as well. Those belong to the KS-1868 site list.

## Fix class

Not chosen by the gate. A revoke that cannot reach the database should not answer success; how it should behave (refuse and leave memory unrevoked, or accept and retry) is the same availability-against-fail-closed ruling as KS-1958.

## Limits

Not tested: a real restart, a real Postgres, the revoke route over HTTP beyond the route dispatch used by the sibling suites, Node 24. Related, not the same defect: KS-1295 (`store()` falls back to memory silently), KS-1684 (the creator refused on the memory fallback after a revoke), KS-1899 (`revoke()` has no ownership check of its own).

title: GDPR erasure: a failed kyc or wallet-connector user.erased step leaves the subject's data in place and nothing reports it (dead-letter unread; request already marked completed)
description:
**BLUF:** When the kyc or wallet-connector `user.erased` handler fails, the erasure is left silently incomplete and nobody is told. The shared event bus tries the handler 3 times back to back, then writes one dead-letter entry with the constant text `Failed after 3 attempts` and acknowledges the message. Nothing reads the dead-letter stream and no retry job exists. The data-subject request was already marked completed: originate's erasure marks it completed at step 12, before it publishes `user.erased` at step 13. What stays behind is the subject's data in that service, as measured below.

**What survives, measured by QA gate 147** (the real kyc `index.ts` and wallet-connector `server.ts` handlers through the real shared `EventBus` subscribe loop, with only the database and the bus's Redis client replaced; the subject has one verification, three document images, one consent with IP address and user agent; a second user's rows are never touched). kyc's four deletes run in this order with no transaction: select verifications, delete images by id, delete images by user id, delete consents, delete verifications, then evict the subject key. Each attempt re-runs the whole sequence.

| failure point (fails on every attempt) | attempts | dead-letter entries | left after the dead-letter (images / consents / verifications) |
| -- | -- | -- | -- |
| kyc: delete images by id | 3 | 1 | 3 / 1 / 1 (everything) |
| kyc: delete consents | 3 | 1 | 0 / 1 / 1 |
| kyc: delete verifications | 3 | 1 | 0 / 0 / 1 |
| wallet-connector: delete sessions | 3 | 1 | every session row for the address |

A failure on the first attempt only (consents once, or the wallet delete once) completes on the second attempt and leaves nothing. By schema (`migrations/002_*.sql` lines 474 to 533 and 813 to 820): the surviving kyc verification holds `provider_application_id`, `provider_check_id`, `liveness_score`, `overall_score`, `risk_level`, `status`, `review_notes` and `documents`; the consent holds the IP address, user agent and timestamps; wallet-connector rows hold the address, wallet type and connected time, all plaintext. Columns written under the subject key (`d1:` envelopes such as `documents` and `review_notes`) are crypto-shredded by originate's step 11. Legacy `v<N>:` kyc rows are under the platform keyring and stay decryptable; that is the same class as `KS-1953`, a different erasure gap (originate lifecycle rows).

**Not new (measured):** an ORDINARY Error at develop's base already leaves exactly this state. PR 1963 (the thrown-value guard on both handlers) does not cause it; it only makes the unreadable-value case behave like the ordinary one (same attempts, same rows erased and left, same dead-letter entry).

**Suggested fix shapes (the gate's, not a decision):**

* a dead-letter consumer or alarm that reopens or flags the data-subject request per service;
* a backoff between attempts, or a re-delivery schedule, instead of three immediate tries;
* wrap kyc's deletes in `transaction()` (the service's `db.ts` already has one) so a failure leaves all or nothing;
* record per-service cascade completion against the request.

**Related (pre-existing, read from source, not run):**

* kyc `dbDeleteUserData` returns 0 when `isDbAvailable()` is false (`index.ts` line 373). The handler then logs `handled` and the bus acknowledges: an erasure silently skipped with no dead-letter. wallet-connector's handler never clears `memConnectedWallets`, so in-memory sessions for the address persist until a restart (gate finding G147-F3).
* The `user.erased` stream entry (user id, request id, `performedBy`, wallet address) is acknowledged but never deleted: `publish` has no XDEL or MAXLEN. A dead-letter copies the raw event into `secuura:events:dead-letter`. So the subject's wallet address stays in Redis after an erasure, whether it succeeded or not (gate finding G147-F4).

**Not tested:** a real Redis (the stream, consumer group, pending list, redelivery after a crash between attempts and the acknowledgement, recovery from a missing group); a real Postgres (the real SQL semantics and the foreign-key cascade are modelled; the timing of the three attempts); a booted service, and the admin HTTP delete path at kyc `index.ts` line 1224, which calls `dbDeleteUserData` directly; originate's publish side end to end; the auth, m365 and other `user.erased` subscribers; backups; Node 24 (host Node v26.8.1).

**Found by:** QA gate 147 on PR 1963, 2026-11-03 (verdict finding G147-F1: HIGH, pre-existing, measured; not caused by `KS-1868`'s PR 1963, not a merge block).

title: transfer approval sweep: when the workflow reads fail, every overdue step is marked timed_out (terminal), including steps set to escalate, so escalations are silently lost
description:
**BLUF:** In the transfer service's escalation sweep (`processEscalations` in `Blockchain/Dev/services/transfer/src/services/approvalWorkflowService.ts`), when the reads that look up a step's workflow fail, every overdue pending step is marked `timed_out`, including steps configured to auto-escalate. `timed_out` is terminal: a later sweep does not select it again and `processApproval` refuses a step that is not pending, so the escalation is silently lost and running the sweep again cannot repair it.

**Cause:** `findWorkflowByStepId` (line 670) reads the workflows through `dbGetActiveWorkflows` (line 238, with a bare `catch { return []; }` at line 243) and then a second `SELECT * FROM svc_approval_workflows` whose failure is swallowed by a bare `catch { /* fall back to active-only */ }`. If both reads fail the workflow is `undefined`, so `stepDef` is `undefined`, the test `stepDef?.autoEscalate && stepDef.escalateTo && !instance.escalatedAt` (line 611) is false, and the `else` branch (lines 622 to 625) sets `status = 'timed_out'`. (The gate cites lines 235 to 243 and 695 to 698 at the PR head; the lines above are at develop `4d1ab2cb6574`, so cite by function name.)

**Measured by QA gate 146** (the REAL transfer service booted as its own Node process for every cell, the real routes and authentication; only the `pg` module replaced, by an in-memory model of the two workflow tables with a unique-id upsert). Setup: 4 overdue pending steps; I1 and I3 on a custom step with `autoEscalate`, `escalateTo: boss-user` and `timeoutHours: 1`; I2 and I4 on the default `step-1`, which times out; `POST /api/workflows/escalate` as a platform administrator. Cell `sweep_wfread`, with the workflow reads failing: the answer is 200 with `{ escalatedCount: 0, timedOutCount: 4 }`. I1 and I3, which should escalate to boss-user, are marked `timed_out`, and a second POST cannot repair them. The result is the same at develop's base and at PR 1962's head, for every kind of failure value including an ordinary Error.

**Effect on approval:** the state refuses rather than grants. The transfer's own execute path gates on the transfer record, not on step instances (`index.ts` lines 802 to 814, read, not run), so nothing this sweep writes can let a transfer proceed. What is lost is the escalation to the named escalation user.

**Suggested fix shape (the gate's, not a decision):** when the step's workflow cannot be found, skip the row and leave it `pending` instead of marking it `timed_out`.

**Related:** a sweep that fails part-way answers `200 success: true` with partial counts and no error indicator (gate finding G146-F4; pre-existing, true at base for an ordinary Error and now for an unreadable value too). The admin caller cannot tell the sweep was incomplete; only a log line says so. Also KS-1881 (the route's platform-admin check, Done) and KS-1868 (PR 1962, unrelated cause).

**Not tested:** a real PostgreSQL (the store is a model; the real WHERE and ON CONFLICT semantics are emulated, not executed); pgbouncer or a mid-statement connection loss; the api-gateway hop to the escalate route (whether and how it is proxied is not traced); a production-mode boot; multi-tenancy pools; Node 24 (host Node v26.8.1).

**Found by:** QA gate 146 on PR 1962, 2026-11-03 (verdict finding G146-F3: recommended follow-up, pre-existing, measured, base = head for every value including an ordinary Error). PR 1962 does not cause it.

title: originate GDPR erasure: a lifecycle event row skipped by the erasure sweep stays decryptable under the platform keyring after the erasure reports completed
description:
**BLUF:** In originate's GDPR erasure, a lifecycle event row that the sweep skips keeps the subject's email recoverable by anyone holding the platform keyring, in live data and in backups, after an erasure that reports `success: true` with the data-subject request marked completed. Step 11 destroys only the subject's own data key (the DEK); lifecycle payloads are encrypted under the platform-wide `v<N>:` keyring (`encodeLifecyclePayload` calls `encryptField`, `Blockchain/Dev/services/originate/src/utils/lifecyclePayloadCodec.ts` lines 34 to 38), not under it. Step 5d skips a row when `decodeLifecyclePayload` reports `payloadUnavailable` (`Blockchain/Dev/services/originate/src/services/gdprService.ts` lines 688 to 690). The deletion log and the DSR record say nothing about the skipped row; the only trace is one error line carrying the event id.

**Not new (measured):** an ORDINARY decrypt error at develop's base already leaves the same row in the same state (a key version that is not loaded). PR 1961 (the thrown-value guard) does not cause this. It routes the unreadable-value case into that same ordinary state; before it, a hostile throw aborted the whole erasure loudly (`success: false`, DSR left open), and that abort was not atomic: the earlier steps and rows had already been written. The old state was also not a real remedy, because a retry hits the same row and aborts again (read, not run).

**Measured by QA gate 145** (the real `executeErasure`, the real lifecycle codec, the real `SubjectDekProvider`, real AES-GCM `encryptField` / `decryptField` / `encryptFieldWithDek` with keys generated in-process, the real winston logger; only the database replaced by an in-memory SQL stand-in). E2 is a lifecycle row holding the subject's email whose decrypt fails; after the erasure the whole platform keyring (v1 + v2) is loaded and E2 is tried.

| version | failure on row E2 | erasure result | DSR completed | subject DEK destroyed | row E2 rewritten | E2 decrypts with the platform keyring | E2 still holds the subject email |
| -- | -- | -- | -- | -- | -- | -- | -- |
| base | none (control) | success | yes | yes | yes | yes | no |
| base | ordinary decrypt error | success | yes | yes | no | yes | YES |
| base | unreadable thrown value | `success: false` ("Erasure failed") | no | no (DEK still live) | no | yes | YES |
| head (PR 1961) | none (control) | success | yes | yes | yes | yes | no |
| head (PR 1961) | ordinary decrypt error | success | yes | yes | no | yes | YES |
| head (PR 1961) | unreadable thrown value | success | yes | yes | no | yes | YES |

Head with an unreadable value equals base with an ordinary error in every column. In the success rows the log says `Erasure completed`; the deletion log does not mention E2.

**Why step 11 cannot shred it:** `executeErasureImpl` step 11 (`gdprService.ts` lines 893 to 894) calls `subjectDeks.destroyDek(userId)`, which sets the wrapped DEK to NULL in `pii_subject_keys` (`Blockchain/Dev/packages/shared/src/crypto/subjectDek.ts`). No lifecycle payload depends on that key. The shared module's own comment in `Blockchain/Dev/packages/shared/src/crypto/encryptedField.ts` says the `v<N>:` format "makes single-subject erasure impossible to guarantee in backups (there is no per-subject key to destroy)". After a completed erasure the skipped row can still be decrypted by `listLifecycleEvents` (`lifecycleEventRepo.ts` line 138, tenant-scoped document listing), which would show the email to whoever can list that document's events (read, not run).

**Retry does not reach it (read, not run):** `payloadUnavailable` is read only at line 690. A second erasure looks up the subject email at step 5c from a users row that step 10 already set to a placeholder of the form `deleted_<id>` at the `anonymized.local` domain, so it cannot match the address inside E2, and nothing else revisits the row.

**Suggested fix shapes (the gate's, not a decision):**

* (a) count skipped rows, and do not mark the DSR plainly `completed` while any remain; record them in the deletion log as `skipped` with the event ids; and/or
* (b) move lifecycle payloads to the subject-DEK (`d1:`) envelope so that step 11 shreds them, as the KS-291 design does for users, consents and DSRs.

**Not tested:** the live PR body; a real Postgres or Prisma client (the SQL stand-in answers by statement prefix, so the real SQL semantics of the other steps are not exercised); a real Key Vault or production keyring (keys were generated in-process); whether a real decrypt ever throws an unreadable value (none is known; Node crypto throws Errors); the HTTP routes (`POST /api/gdpr/erasure/:userId`, `executeErasureByExternalRef`) and a booted service; a second erasure run against the same subject; `listLifecycleEvents`; backups; Node 24 (host Node v26.8.1).

**Related:** KS-537 (lifecycle payload encryption and erasure), KS-291 (the subject-DEK design for users, consents and DSRs), KS-1868 (PR 1961, unrelated cause).

**Found by:** QA gate 145 on PR 1961, 2026-11-03 (verdict finding G145-F1: recommended follow-up, HIGH priority for data protection, pre-existing, measured).

title: api-gateway: with Redis unavailable, enforceDocumentTypeRules passes every document (catalogue reads empty), so MFA-required types are allowed
description:
**BLUF:** When `isRedisAvailable()` is false (every Redis outage: an ordinary error on the client, a socket `close`, or the 4th retry), `enforceDocumentTypeRules` (`Blockchain/Dev/services/api-gateway/src/services/enforcement.ts`, called at `routes/verification.ts` line 856) reads an EMPTY document-type catalogue on every replica (`documentTypesStore` is only written while the flag is false), `resolveDocumentType` returns null, and the "catalogue empty" branch returns `{ ok: true, docType: {} }`. A document type registered with `requireMFA: true` is then allowed.

**Measured by QA gate 144** (real `redis.ts`, `enforcement.ts` and winston; only `ioredis` replaced; two replicas sharing one store): a type registered with `requireMFA: true` is REFUSED with 403 `MFA_REQUIRED` while the flag is true, and ALLOWED on both replicas while the flag is false, with Redis up or down, at develop's base AND at PR 1960's head after an ordinary Error. Evidence: `logs/probe_site3_table.log`, enforce block, rows `base trigger=ordinary` and `head trigger=ordinary`: `ALLOWED ok:true docType={}` on replica A and B, with `down=0` and `down=1`.

**By reading, not run:** the same pass-through skips the `isActive` check, the verification-level check (`creatorVerificationLevel`), the auth-provider check (`allowedAuthProviders`), the metadata-schema check (`metadataSchema`) and the approval-workflow gate (`createWorkflowInstanceIfRequired` sees no `requiresApproval`).

**Where it sits at develop** `4d1ab2cb6574`**, read by the filer:** `resolveDocumentType` calls `redisService.getAllDocumentTypes()` at `enforcement.ts` line 72; `enforceDocumentTypeRules` reads the catalogue again at line 126 and returns `{ ok: true, docType: {} }` at lines 117 and 137, where the code comment says an empty catalogue means "never seeded, or Redis TTL expiry". The gate cites `enforcement.ts` lines 78 and 128; the statements I read are at lines 72 and 126, so cite them by function name.

**Reach:** every Redis blip in production puts the gateway in this state (an ordinary error, `close`, or retry 4). PR 1960 (the `redis.ts` error listener and `initRedis` catch) does not cause it and does not change it; it makes the unreadable-value path land in the same state an ordinary Error already reaches.

**Not tested:** a real Redis or `ioredis` client (a stand-in was used; the `ioredis` emit, close and retry path was read in `node_modules` 5.11.1, not run); a booted gateway over HTTP (the middleware and `enforceDocumentTypeRules` were called directly); `createWorkflowInstanceIfRequired` and the `isActive`, verification-level, provider and schema skips under fallback (read, only the MFA rule was run); admin routes in fallback; Node 24 (host Node v26.8.1).

**Related:** KS-1256, KS-1540, KS-1532, KS-1627 (readers of the same flag); KS-1466 (untyped creates never meet the catalogue's document rules: a different defect); KS-1868 (PR 1960, unrelated cause).

**Found by:** QA gate 144 on PR 1960, 2026-11-03 (verdict finding G144-F1: recommended follow-up, HIGH, pre-existing, measured).

title: staking: POST /api/stake takes address and amount from the caller, so any signed-in user can create or grow a stake position for any address
description:
**BLUF:** `POST /api/stake` (`services/staking/src/routes/stake.ts:189-245`) takes `address` and `amount` from the request body and saves a stake position for that address with no ownership or chain check. By the same shape, the unstake routes (`POST /api/stake/unstake` `:263`, `POST /api/stake/complete-unstake` `:317`) also take the address from the body; they were not read line by line. So any signed-in caller can create or grow a stake position for any address. `txHash` is optional and is logged but never verified. KS 1942's design treats `svc_stake_positions` as NOT a trusted stake source for this reason.

## Where (develop `0e3a9b65cdd6`; read from source, NOT run)

* Mount: `services/staking/src/index.ts:80` applies `jwtAuthenticate()` to `/api`, and `:82` mounts the stake routes at `/api/stake`. Any signed-in caller reaches them.
* `routes/stake.ts:189-245`: the handler parses `StakeSchema` from `req.body` (`:191`), takes `{ address, amount, txHash }` (`:196`), loads the position for that address (`:199`), adds `amount` to it or creates it (`:213-228`), and saves it (`:230`). It also adds to the in-process pool stats (`:233-236`).
* `req.user` is not read anywhere in `routes/stake.ts`. `txHash` is optional in the schema (`:33`), and its only other use is the log line (`:243`).

## Why it matters

KS 1942 (the governance register route takes stake from the caller) is being fixed by making stake and roles admin-set only. Its design rejected `svc_stake_positions` as a stake source because this route lets any caller assert any position.

## Not checked

The unstake and complete-unstake handlers line by line. Whether the gateway restricts `/api/stake` to a role. Whether any client other than the tests calls these routes. Whether the Aiken staking validator is meant to be the source of truth (no service reads it).

## Related

KS 1942 (governance register route, same class). KS 1845 (covers only the admin listing `GET /api/stake/all`, not these routes).

## Searched first

Board search over issue content and comment bodies:

* "svc_stake_positions" and "routes/stake.ts" find KS 1845 (an issue covering only `GET /api/stake/all`) and a KS 1544 comment.
* "POST /api/stake" finds comments on KS 188, KS 256 and KS 492, about business-rule refusals and OpenAPI examples on `/unstake` and `/complete-unstake`, not ownership.
* "StakeSchema" and "staking service" find 0.
* Control: "minProposalStake" finds KS 1940.

## Found by

Seat F 23rd while designing KS 1942; filed on the coordinator's ruling (D4). Not measured against a running service.

title: originate retention sweep: one unreadable thrown value stops the whole sweep and the later policies' deletions are skipped (gdprService.ts lines 499 and 503)
description:
**BLUF:** in the retention sweep (`enforceRetentionImpl` in `Blockchain/Dev/services/originate/src/services/gdprService.ts`) the per-policy catch (line 499) and the outer catch (line 503) read the thrown value with `err instanceof Error ? err.message : String(err)` inside the `logger.error` call, unguarded. If one policy's DELETE rejects with a value whose read throws (a revoked Proxy; an Error whose `message` getter throws), that read throws inside the catch, the exception leaves the loop, and every LATER policy is skipped for that run: no DELETE or anonymisation, no `data_deletion_log` row, no `last_enforcement_at` update. With an ordinary Error or a string the sweep logs `Retention enforcement failed` and continues. A GDPR deletion obligation is silently not met for that run. Pre-existing; found by gate 104 on pull request 1923 (not in it); measured equal at base and head of that pull request.

* **Where (read at develop 86e12156d4e0):** lines 498 to 500, `} catch (err: any) { logger.error('Retention enforcement failed', { dataType: policy.data_type, error: err instanceof Error ? err.message : String(err) }); }`, and lines 502 to 504, `logger.error('Retention enforcement error', { error: err instanceof Error ? err.message : String(err) })`. The sweep runs from the background retention scheduler and from the SYSTEM_ADMIN route `POST /api/gdpr/retention/enforce` (comment at lines 429 to 435).
* **Measured (gate 104, probe R2; not my measurement):** the real `enforceRetention` over a database stand-in holding three policies (`user_sessions`, `verification_requests`, `share_records`). Ordinary Error and string, policy 1 or policy 2 failing: the later policies' DELETE, deletion-log INSERT and `last_enforcement_at` update all run. Revoked Proxy or throwing getter: a failure on policy 1 skipped 2 policies and a failure on policy 2 skipped 1; line 503 then logs the new TypeError (or the getter's Error). The same at the base and at the head of pull request 1923, which does not touch this file.
* **Fix shape:** at both lines `let reason: string; try { reason = err instanceof Error ? err.message : String(err); } catch { reason = 'unreadable thrown value'; }`, then log `{ dataType: policy.data_type, error: reason }` and `{ error: reason }`. Add one cell asserting that policy 2's DELETE still runs after policy 1 rejects with a revoked Proxy (red at the base, green after). The same unguarded form is at 14 more lines of this file by my regex (227, 242, 314, 377, 647, 917, 978, 988, 998, 1008, 1018, 1028, 1588, 1603; the gate counted 17); I have not read them.
* **Not shown:** whether an unreadable value can reach this DELETE in practice (Prisma rejects with Error subclasses); the gate's values are synthetic.
* **Related:** KS 1868 (the umbrella; no pass or brief covers `gdprService.ts`). A board search by path and words (`gdprService.ts`, `retention sweep`, `enforceRetention`, `enforceRetentionImpl`, `Retention enforcement failed`, `last_enforcement_at`), with a positive control, found no ticket for it.

title: api-gateway: ORG_ADMIN and ISSUER_ADMIN can set any user's verification level (tenant bound unmeasured)
description:
**BLUF:** In the api-gateway, `PATCH /api/admin/identity/users/:id/level` sits behind `requireAdmin`, and `requireAdmin` admits `ORG_ADMIN` and `ISSUER_ADMIN` (and the lower-case `issuer_admin`). A probe with a stub database showed both roles reach the handler and issue `UPDATE users SET verification_level = $1 ... WHERE id = $2::uuid` for ANY user id. The SQL has no tenant or organisation predicate. **Whether row-level security (or anything else) stops those two roles from changing a user in another tenant was NOT run**, so this is an open question, not a confirmed cross-tenant write. A real-PostgreSQL probe with a cross-tenant id settles it.

## What is read in the code (develop `d9acf71a3fcc`, `Blockchain/Dev/services/api-gateway/src/routes/admin.ts`)

* `:600` `const ADMIN_ROLES = ['SYSTEM_ADMIN', 'system_admin', 'super_admin', 'SUPER_ADMIN', 'platform_admin', 'ORG_ADMIN', 'ISSUER_ADMIN', 'issuer_admin'];`
* `:602-:605` a comment (KS 458) says platform-level admins read across tenants and that "ORG_ADMIN / ISSUER_ADMIN keep the tenant-scoped view the policy now enforces (their request ALS context applies)". `PLATFORM_SCOPE_ROLES` (`:606`) lists only the five platform roles, and `adminScope` (`:607-:610`) runs a query under the platform scope for those five only.
* `:612-:651` `requireAdmin` checks the token and then only `ADMIN_ROLES.includes(role)`; a role outside the list gets 403. It does not look at the target user, the caller's organisation or the caller's tenant.
* `:1313` `router.patch('/api/admin/identity/users/:id/level', requireAdmin, mockBodyParser, ...)`. The body's `verificationLevel` must be one of NONE, BASIC, SOCIAL, STANDARD, ENHANCED, HIGH, GOVERNMENT (anything else answers 400 with no query).
* `:1322-:1325` `adminScope(req, () => query('UPDATE users SET verification_level = $1, updated_at = NOW() WHERE id = $2::uuid RETURNING id, verification_level', [verificationLevel, id]))`. The only predicate is the user id. `rowCount === 0` answers 404.

## Source and its limit

Found by gate 98 (the QA gate on pull request 1916, the KS 1868 `admin.ts` catch-read change), finding G98-F4, 2026-11-02. It ran the real admin router (real `createAdminRoutes`, real `requireAdmin`, real `ADMIN_ROLES`) on a loopback listener with only the token verifier, the database, the logger and redis replaced. Its auth matrix: no token 401, a plain USER 403, and ORG_ADMIN, ISSUER_ADMIN and SYSTEM_ADMIN each 200 with exactly one query, `UPDATE users SET verification_level = $1`, parameters the level and the id. **The database was a stub, so row-level security was not run.** The behaviour is pre-existing and unchanged by pull request 1916 (that change only guards how a thrown value is read for a log line). Filed on Wednesday's commission from that note; I read the code lines above at `d9acf71a3fcc`, and I did not run anything against a database.

## What is not known, and what would settle it

1. **Cross-tenant.** Does the tenant row-level security on `users` reject the UPDATE when an `ORG_ADMIN` or `ISSUER_ADMIN` of tenant A names a user of tenant B? Settle with a real PostgreSQL carrying the project's RLS policies and migrations: two tenants, a user in B, a token for an `ORG_ADMIN` of A, `PATCH` the level for B's user. 404 (zero rows) means RLS bounds the call; 200 and a changed row means it does not.
2. **Same tenant, other organisation.** Tenant row-level security does not know organisations, so an `ORG_ADMIN` or `ISSUER_ADMIN` may be able to change the level of a user in a different organisation of the SAME tenant. Not measured either way. The policy question of which roles may cross an organisation boundary is KS 1535 and the role-list drift is KS 1536; neither covers this route.
3. **What a changed level buys.** The board's KS 1176 and KS 1190 describe the gateway's `meetsVerificationLevel` checks on this value. Which routes read the stored level for an access decision was not traced here.

## Board search (so nobody files this twice)

Run 2026-11-02 over this team's issues and comment bodies for `admin/identity`, `identity/users`, `/level`, `verification_level`, `requireAdmin`, `ADMIN_ROLES`, `ORG_ADMIN` and `ISSUER_ADMIN`; positive control KS 1865 found. The route terms hit only the KS 1868 umbrella's own comments; the symbol terms hit tickets about other routes. Closest, and not covering this route: KS 1536 (role vocabularies), KS 1584 (an organisation-bound escape through a provisioning key), KS 1855 (gateway admin stand-ins).

## Not in scope

No change to `admin.ts` is proposed or made here. Severity is not asserted: priority High is the commissioning call, pending the probe above.

title: Billing: addCertificationCredits' optimistic lock is not a compare-and-set, so one call can credit twice under a concurrent write
description:
**BLUF:** `StripeService.addCertificationCredits` keeps the credit balance in Stripe customer metadata and calls its read-update-verify loop "optimistic locking", but Stripe's customer update is unconditional, so the loop is not a compare-and-set. When a concurrent writer changes the balance between this call's update and its verify read, the loop re-reads and adds the credits AGAIN, so one call can credit twice; a write can also be lost. Read in code, not run. It is the same money class as KS-1933 (one purchase credited more than once), through a different door.

**Where** (`services/billing/src/services/stripeService.ts` at PR 1913's head `5d6bd74daa3e`)

* `addCertificationCredits` (:226-247): up to 3 attempts of retrieve (:229), compute `currentBalance + credits` (:231-232), `customers.update` with the new `certificationCredits` (:234-236), retrieve again (:239); if the read-back is not the value it wrote, it logs a conflict (:244) and goes round again from a fresh read.
* `useCertificationCredits` (:252-278) has the same loop for debits.

**A sequence that credits twice (worked from the code):** the balance is 10. Call A (+5) and call B (+3) both read 10. A writes 15, B writes 13 (A's write is lost). A's verify reads 13, not 15: A retries, reads 13, writes 18, verify passes. B's verify reads 18, not 13: B retries, reads 18, writes 21, verify passes. The final 21 is 10 + 5 + 3 + 3: B's credit landed twice.

**Not in scope here:** no fix is designed or built in KS-1933's pull request (KS-1933 adds a per-payment ledger in PostgreSQL that stops a second CALL for the same purchase; it does not change what one call does). Found by Seat F 22nd while tracing KS-1933 (Wednesday's ANSWER of 2026-11-02 commissioned this filing).

**Related:** KS-1933.

title: Billing: one Stripe purchase can be credited more than once (two events, post-grant retry, finalise/release catches)
description:
**BLUF:** One Stripe purchase can add certification credits to a customer's balance twice. QA gate 95 (Opus, 2026-11-02) ran the real billing webhooks router with only the database and the Stripe service replaced, and measured three ways it happens plus two catch blocks that either re-grant or strand a paid event. Kam ruled on 2026-11-02: the fix is designed and tested in code and goes through the QA gate; nothing is deployed without his tap. Whether the live Stripe endpoint sends both events (case 1) is Kam's own check; no agent has read it.

**What gate 95 measured** (`services/billing/src/routes/webhooks.ts` at PR 1913's head `5d6bd74daa3e`; line numbers are that file's)

1. **Two events, one purchase.** A `checkout.session.completed` and a `payment_intent.succeeded` for the same purchase, both carrying `certifications: '5'` and no `creditsAdded` flag, delivered clean: **2 grants**, with and without PR 1913. The `webhook_events` claim is keyed by the Stripe event id and the two events have different ids, so the claim does not dedupe them. `handlePaymentSucceeded` skips when `paymentIntent.metadata.creditsAdded` is set, but nothing in the code writes that key.
2. **Ordinary Error thrown after the grant** (for example a logger call after `addCertificationCredits` has returned): the claim is released, Stripe redelivers, **2 grants**, with and without PR 1913.
3. **Unreadable thrown value after the grant:** 1 grant today, only because the request crashes and the event is stranded; **2 grants with PR 1913**, the same as an ordinary Error.
4. `finaliseEvent`**'s catch (:110-111)** reads `err?.message` unguarded and runs after the grant: an unreadable rejection gives **2 grants**, against 1 for an ordinary Error.
5. `releaseClaim`**'s catch (:129-135)** reads `err?.message` unguarded: an unreadable rejection leaves the row `processing`, the redelivery is acknowledged as a duplicate, **0 grants** for a paid event.

**Limits of the measurement:** a stand-in database (a model of the claim, release and finalise statements) and a stand-in Stripe service. No real PostgreSQL, no real Stripe, no booted service, no read of the live Stripe endpoint's event subscriptions. The unreadable thrown values in cases 3 to 5 are synthetic.

**Where the credits live:** the balance is the Stripe customer's metadata field `certificationCredits`, written by `StripeService.addCertificationCredits` (`services/billing/src/services/stripeService.ts:226-247`). PostgreSQL holds only `webhook_events`.

**Ruling:** Kam, 2026-11-02, decision `secuura-billing-possible-double-credit-two-stripe-events-1102`, option a: file a ticket; a Claude seat designs and tests a fix that makes one purchase credit exactly once, through the QA gate, nothing deployed; Kam checks the Stripe endpoint's event list once.

**Related:** KS-1868 (the catch-site umbrella; the catches in cases 4 and 5 are KS-1868 sites). PR 1913 in Secuura/Distributed_Secuura (billing webhook catches; gate 95 = GO WITH NOTES; its merge is held until this fix is gated).
